answer.reason: The pool only ever holds one task, which has either finished or already been cancelled by future.cancel() when shutdown runs. So cancel_futures has nothing queued to cancel, and no success, error or timeout path behaves differently.

Removing pool.shutdown only changes worker-thread cleanup. On timeout, the original shutdown(wait=False) never waited, so both versions stop waiting and raise TimeoutError at once. On success, the idle worker is freed by garbage collection instead of an explicit join. Only a short-lived thread-count difference is observable, and the requirement does not ask about that.

Removing `future.cancel()` changes nothing the contract can see. A future that has already started running can't be cancelled, and one still pending is cancelled anyway by the following `pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)`. Either way, the mutant stops waiting, raises the same TimeoutError and hands control to fallback in the same way; the only difference is a tiny scheduling race that no requirement observes.

After a timeout, the mutant leaves timed_out False, so the finally block calls pool.shutdown(wait=True) and blocks until the timed-out executor call finishes. The sync path therefore keeps waiting on the timed-out route, against the requirement that it stop waiting. The existing tests likely pass only because their slow executor returns soon anyway.
